q: What should an as-is process map show?
options: How work is really done today, including workarounds
How the procedure manual says work should be done
Only the steps performed by the system
why: The as-is map must reflect reality, workarounds included, or the analysis will be wrong.

q: Differences between the as-is and to-be processes are called…
why: Gap analysis identifies what must change; each gap becomes a requirement, process change or training need.

q: What is the first step when mapping a process?
options: Define the scope: the trigger where it starts and the outcome where it ends
why: Scoping the start and end prevents the map from growing endlessly.

q: Which audience typically needs a level 2–3 (detailed) process model?
why: Detailed models with decisions and exceptions are needed to build and test the solution; executives want high-level views.

q: Why add measures such as time per step and error rate to an as-is map?
options: They turn opinions into facts and show where to improve
They make the diagram look professional
They replace the need for interviews
why: Data quantifies pain points and provides a baseline to prove improvement later.

q: In a flowchart, what does a diamond represent?
why: Diamonds are decisions (questions with labeled outcomes).

q: What does each arrow that crosses from one swimlane to another represent?
options: A handoff between roles, a common source of delay and error
why: Handoffs are visible in swimlane diagrams and are often where waiting and errors happen.

q: Which activity name follows good practice?
why: Activities should be named verb + noun.

q: In a flowchart, an oval represents…
why: Ovals (terminators) mark the start and end points.

q: Who maintains the BPMN standard?
why: BPMN 2.0 is an OMG standard.

q: In BPMN, an exclusive (XOR) gateway means…
options: Exactly one outgoing path is taken
All paths are taken in parallel
One or more paths may be taken
why: XOR: exactly one path, based on a condition.

q: After approval, a payment must be posted to the ledger AND a confirmation email sent at the same time. Which gateway models this?
why: A parallel gateway activates all outgoing paths simultaneously.

q: A claim may need a fraud check, a credit check, or both, depending on conditions. Which gateway fits?
why: An inclusive gateway takes one or more paths depending on conditions.

q: In BPMN, how are messages between two separate organizations (pools) shown?
why: Message flows cross pools. Sequence flows stay inside a pool.

q: A BPMN circle with a thick border represents…
why: Start events are thin circles, intermediate events double circles, and end events thick circles.

q: In BPMN, a pool usually represents ___ and a lane represents ___.
options: a major participant such as an organization; a role or department within it
why: Pools are participants such as 'Bank' and 'Customer'; lanes divide a pool into roles.

q: A task with a small '+' marker in BPMN is…
why: The '+' marker indicates a sub-process containing more detail.

q: What does SIPOC stand for?
why: A SIPOC is a high-level process view used to agree scope.

q: A break takes 5 days end to end but only 40 minutes of actual work. What does a value stream map reveal?
options: Most of the lead time is waiting, which is waste to remove
The analysts are working too slowly
why: Low process cycle efficiency (process time ÷ lead time) shows waiting is the main opportunity.

q: Process cycle efficiency is calculated as…
options: Number of steps ÷ number of people
why: It's the proportion of total elapsed time that is spent adding value.

q: What does a UML use case diagram show?
options: Actors and the goals they achieve with the system, within a system boundary
The detailed order of screen clicks
why: Use case diagrams are scope pictures showing actors and use cases, not flows.

q: Which UML diagram best shows the messages exchanged between the ledger system and the reconciliation engine over time?
why: Sequence diagrams show interactions between participants in time order.

q: A break moves through Open → Under investigation → Approved → Closed. Which diagram models this best?
why: State diagrams show an object's states and the events that cause transitions.

q: In a use case diagram, «include» means…
options: The base use case always uses the included use case
The use case is out of scope
why: «include» is mandatory reused behavior; «extend» is optional behavior under conditions.

q: One account has many transactions. What cardinality is this?
why: A single account relates to many transaction records.

q: What does a primary key do?
options: Uniquely identifies each record in a table
why: A primary key is unique for each row. A foreign key references another table.

q: A context diagram (level 0 DFD) shows…
options: The whole system as one process with its external entities and data flows
why: Context diagrams agree system scope by showing what goes in and out.

q: Which artifact defines each field's meaning, type, allowed values and example?
why: A data dictionary documents the definition and rules of each data element.

q: Why are decision tables useful for complex business rules?
options: They make sure every combination of conditions has a defined action
why: Decision tables make rules complete and easy to test.

q: Which is the best practice when mapping a process with stakeholders?
options: Draw it live with the people who do the work so they can correct it
Draw it alone and email it for sign-off
why: Collaborative modeling surfaces errors and builds ownership.

q: Why keep the as-is model after the to-be is approved?
options: To measure improvement against the baseline
It is legally required in all countries
To reuse it as the to-be
why: The as-is (with its measures) is the baseline for proving the change delivered value.
